first.rationale: Two of the three current problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) sit directly on the onboarding path, so simplify_onboarding is the single lever that touches both, whereas promotional_pricing addresses only the competitive symptom and referral/enterprise levers address neither declining metric. I am verifying memory_86 because it is the direct basis for the intended action and its consolidated form reports only proxy outcomes (completion rate, time-to-value) with no statement about qualified revenue or retention — I need the original record to see segment, duration, and whether revenue quality was ever measured. I am verifying memory_73 because it is the most tempting alternative under competitor pressure and carries the largest unstated downside: discount-led acquisition can import price-sensitive, low-retention accounts, and 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' in a summary may be short-horizon gross revenue, not sustainable qualified revenue. Key downstream risk I am explicitly carrying forward: memory_31's 'cut required fields' finding means activation lift may have been bought by admitting lower-intent signups, which would degrade qualified revenue even while the headline metric improves; if verification shows memory_86 rests on the same mechanism, I will keep the experiment but gate it on downstream qualification and 30/60-day retention metrics rather than completion rate alone. These memories are consolidated summaries stripped of caveats and are 15-64 days old under changed competitive conditions, so I treat them as directional priors, not settled facts. Standard experiment scale with revenue-quality guardrails rather than broad rollout, since the supporting evidence never demonstrated the outcome the objective actually names.

final.rationale: Verification resolved both open questions in favor of the intended action. exp_86 is stronger than its consolidated summary suggested: it reported not just completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days but 30-day retention +3%, meaning the onboarding lift did not come at the cost of cohort quality. That directly retires the risk I flagged earlier — that shortened onboarding might buy activation by admitting lower-intent accounts. It also transfers well to the current situation, since onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%) are exactly the metrics exp_86 moved. exp_73 was disconfirmed as a sustainable lever in the sharpest possible way: signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% were real, but 30-day retention -12% and the source's explicit conclusion that the cohort does not survive first renewal mean the revenue was borrowed, not earned. Under a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, matching the competitor's entry pricing would manufacture a churn cliff one renewal cycle out and worsen the position I am trying to defend. I am therefore not spending the slot on promotional_pricing despite it being the most direct answer to the competitive pressure. Remaining uncertainty I am not papering over: exp_86's retention signal is 30-day, which is shorter than the renewal horizon where exp_73's damage surfaced, so a +3% at 30 days is encouraging but not proof of durable revenue quality. The archived records are also 24-52 days old and predate the competitor's entry pricing, so the inbound SMB mix this week may be more price-sensitive than the population exp_86 ran on — the effect size could compress even if the direction holds. I am running at standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout for that reason, and instrumenting on downstream qualification and 60-day retention rather than completion rate alone, so that if this lift is being bought from cohort quality the way exp_73's was, it shows up before the change is generalized. memory_31 and memory_91 are used as corroborating priors only; neither was verified and both report proxy metrics without revenue-quality evidence.
